pl-l2d39c3-d1e108.summary: Asks how to take Ambrose on 'I do not what I will': man subject to sin does what he does not will because he naturally wills good, but this will lacks effect unless grace helps and frees. If enslaved to sin he gladly wills and does evil; how then does he naturally will good? Is it the same motion, and which one does grace free when man is justified?

pl-l2d39c3-d1e111.summary: States this is a deep question, answered variously.

pl-l2d39c3-d1e114.summary: Reports some who posit two motions; one by which man naturally wills good, called natural because it was the motion of human nature in its first condition, created without defect, upright in will.
claims: One motion is the natural will for good.

pl-l2d39c3-d1e118.summary: Cites the Ecclesiastical Dogmas: the first humans were created good and upright with free choice, able to sin by their will, and sinned by will, not necessity. So man naturally wills good, being made with a good will: the higher spark of reason, which as Jerome says could not be extinguished even in Cain, always wills good and hates evil.
claims: The spark of reason always wills good.

pl-l2d39c3-d1e129.summary: Reports the other motion, by which the mind abandons the higher law and subjects itself to sins in delight; before grace it reigns and suppresses the other, both being from free choice; when grace comes, the evil motion is crushed and the natural good one freed and helped to will good effectively. Before grace, though man naturally wills good, he should not simply be said to have a good will, but rather an evil one.
claims: Grace frees the natural good motion.

pl-l2d39c3-d1e132.summary: Reports others who say there is one will, one motion, by which man naturally wills good and by vice wills evil and delights in it; good insofar as willing good, evil insofar as willing evil.
claims: Another view: one will with two directions.

pl-l2d39c3.summary: Asks how to understand Ambrose's saying that man subject to sin does what he does not will, because he naturally wills good, though this will lacks effect without grace: is the will by which he gladly serves sin the same motion as that by which he naturally wills good, and which is freed by grace? Some posit two motions: one by which man naturally wills good, as in his first upright condition, the higher spark of reason that, as Jerome says, could not be extinguished even in Cain; and another by which the mind, abandoning the higher law, subjects itself to sins and delights in them, reigning before grace; grace crushes the evil motion and frees the good one. Before grace, man should not simply be said to have a good will. Others posit one will that naturally wills good and by vice wills evil, good insofar as it wills good, evil insofar as it wills evil.
claims: Man subject to sin naturally wills good, but without effect unless grace helps.
Some posit two motions: a natural will for good and a will that serves sin.
The higher spark of reason always wills good and hates evil, even in Cain.
Grace crushes the evil motion and frees the natural good one.
Before grace, man is not simply said to have a good will.
Others posit one will, good in willing good and evil in willing evil.
